nameStory: The radiated shanny gets its name from the radiating pattern of lines or stripes that spread outward from its head and body, like rays of sunlight. 'Shanny' is an old maritime term used by fishermen for small, elongated bottom-dwelling fish that live among rocks and tide pools.
description: The radiated shanny is a small, eel-like fish that belongs to the prickleback family - named for their spiny dorsal fins that run along their backs like tiny prickles. These slender marine fish have elongated bodies that help them squeeze into rocky crevices and seaweed beds along the coast. They're relatively small fish, typically measuring just a few inches in length, making them easy to overlook despite their distinctive radiating stripe patterns.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long and eel-like with a slender, compressed body that feels firm and muscular when gently handled

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Displays distinctive radiating lines or stripes that spread outward from the head area, creating a sunburst-like pattern

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long dorsal fin runs along most of the back with spiny rays that feel prickly to the touch, giving the prickleback family its name

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found hiding in rocky tide pools and among seaweed where they can quickly dart into crevices when disturbed

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish, typically just a few inches long - about the length of your index finger

habitat: Radiated shannies live in the cold waters of the northwestern Atlantic along New England's rocky coastlines. Look for them in tide pools, rocky intertidal zones, and shallow areas with plenty of seaweed and kelp for cover. They prefer areas with hard substrate like granite ledges and boulder fields where they can dart between rocks when threatened.

seasonality.spring: More active as waters begin to warm, often seen darting between rocks during low tide exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be spotted in tide pools and shallow rocky areas during low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper water as coastal temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Less visible as they seek deeper, more protected areas, though some may still be found in sheltered tide pools.

funFact: The radiated shanny is the only fish in its entire genus - it's literally in a class by itself with no close genetic relatives, making it a living evolutionary unique specimen swimming in New England waters!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small tide pool fish like rock gunnels or other pricklebacks, but the radiated shanny's distinctive radiating stripe pattern spreading from the head is unique - think of it as nature's own sunburst design that no other local fish displays.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'shanny,' this fish isn't closely related to true shannies but got the name from old fishing terminology. The prickleback family name can be misleading - while their fins are spiny, they're not dangerously sharp like some fish spines.
compareHints: Since the radiated shanny is the only species in its genus, it's unique among New England pricklebacks. Compared to other prickleback family members like rock gunnels, the radiated shanny is distinguished by its radiating stripe pattern rather than the more uniform coloration or different stripe arrangements seen in its relatives. Its body proportions are also more elongated relative to its depth compared to most other local pricklebacks.
